sense: to move on, or to come back to the point
also: to get back to the point

terms.grammar: phrase: hāctenus, so far and no further
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.24.1–2: sed haec hāctenus. tē ad cēnās itāre dēsīsse molestē ferō
Cic. Att. 16.7.6: sed haec hāctenus; reliqua cōram
terms.comment: Cicero’s way of closing one subject and turning to the next, very frequent in his letters (Lewis & Short: “so much for this”).

terms.gloss: but to get back to the point
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.13.2: sed ut ad rem redeam, tē istīc invītum nōn esse vehementer gaudeō
terms.comment: After a digression. Shorter, sed ad rem redeō (Cic. Att. 5.21.13) or redeāmus ad nostrum (Cic. Att. 7.11.3).

phrases.latin: sed haec hāctenus. tē ad cēnās itāre dēsīsse molestē ferō
phrases.english: but enough of that. I’m sorry you’ve stopped going out to dinner
but enough of that; the rest when we meet.

phrases.latin: sed ut ad rem redeam, tē istīc invītum nōn esse vehementer gaudeō
phrases.english: but to get back to the point, I’m very glad you don’t mind being out there

hactenus.html: The ablative hāc with tenus, which Vergil still writes apart (hāc Trōjāna tenus, Verg. A. 6.62); Lewis & Short marks the same long vowel in quātenus and eātenus.

sources: Lewis & Short: hactenus · Lewis & Short: redeo · Lewis & Short: quatenus
